title: One of those plays that you’ll be thinking about for a while- I am so...
transcript: I saw 250 shows last year, and this play was one of my favorites. And it just began its return engagement at Studio C View off Broadway. So if you missed it last year, you now have another chance. The play is called well, I'll let you go and follows a widow, Maggie, processing the death of her husband, who died under somewhat mysterious circumstances. And the play is a series of one on one conversations between Maggie and people coming to visit her in her grief. And through these conversations, we start to slowly piece together Maggie's relationship with her now deceased husband and what actually happened the night that he died. Maggie is played brilliantly by Quincy Tyler Bernstein. She is giving this wonderfully nuanced performance that at first starts really guarded, but slowly but surely she lets us see the many layers underneath. She is also joined by a stacked ensemble of off Broadway favorites, including Will Dagger, Emily Davis, Constant Schulman, among others. Due to the structure of the play, most of them only get a short 10 minute scene with Quincy and then leave. But even with just that small amount of stage time, all of these characters feel so fully realized. And that is as much a credit to the actors as it is to playwright Bubba Weiler. This is actually his first play after spending many years as an actor, and what a stunning playwriting debut this is. I am already such a Huge fan of his and I cannot wait to see what else he writes. I would also be remiss if I didn't mention director Jack Serio, who has made a bit of a name for himself in the off Broadway space directing these hyper intimate theatrical experiences. And that is definitely true of this show as well. Judy's C B U. Is a tiny 300 seat theater, and they've actually moved some of the seats down onto the stage to make it feel even more intimate. And that intimacy not only makes you feel like a fly on the wall for these very private conversations, it also allows for the actors to give these very naturalistic and subtle performances. So much so that despite the fact that the set is left intentionally very minimal, being composed primarily of folding chairs and tables, play itself. And this production still feels so grounded in a reality that is slowly being built around you. And it is this combination of superb writing, performances, directing that definitely makes, well, I'll let you go, a Broadway Ben must see.
classificationReason: Detailed first-hand review with specific performance analysis (Quincy Tyler Bernstein's nuanced arc) and ensemble commentary; creator saw it previously and again at its return engagement, recommending it to those who missed it.
